title: The Wrong Suspect: Why the C–F Bond Isn't to Blame for PFAS
description: Why the strongest single bond in organic chemistry is probably not the reason PFAS are still here — the chemistry of the C–F bond, how one enzyme has been caught breaking it atom by atom, and why evolution, not thermodynamics, is the real obstacle to degrading PFAS.
coverAlt: Shaban Ahmad at his desk, working to finalise the DeFluorX pipeline
body:
You have almost certainly handled a carbon–fluorine (C–F) bond today: in the coating on a pan, the water-repellent finish on a jacket, the grease-proof lining of a takeaway box, quite possibly in a medicine, since roughly a fifth of marketed pharmaceuticals carry at least one fluorine atom [1]. It is also, with fairly high probability, in your blood.

Industry did not stumble on that persistence by accident; it selected for it. Fluorochemicals were designed to shrug off heat, oxidants, ultraviolet light, acid, base and biology, and they have done precisely what was asked of them. So the bond gets the blame. Open almost any paper on PFAS biodegradation and somewhere in the first paragraph you will find the claim that these compounds persist because the C–F bond is the strongest bond in organic chemistry [2]. It is a tidy explanation, and I think it is also the least useful third of the truth.

## In brief:

- The C–F bond deserves its reputation. At up to about 130 kcal/mol it is the strongest single bond carbon forms [1, 3].
- It also gets stronger the more fluorines sit on the same carbon. Chlorine does the opposite, which explains a lot about why PFAS behave unlike every pollutant we learned on [3].
- A strong bond is not the same as an unreactive molecule. A C–F bond's dissociation energy is not the same thing as the activation barrier an enzyme has to clear, and neither is the same thing as the overall thermodynamics of a full mineralisation pathway; lowering activation barriers is what enzymes do for a living.
- One enzyme family has been watched doing exactly that, at atomic resolution. It does not overpower anything: it lines up a nucleophile, keeps water out, and builds a small pocket that catches the fluoride as it leaves [1].
- So the honest version of the story is less about chemistry than about history. Nothing on Earth ever had a reason to evolve the rest of the machinery around that one step, and the product of the reaction, fluoride, poisons the cell that makes it [2].

## What fluorine does to carbon:

Fluorine is the most electronegative element there is, and also small — the smallest halogen, comparable in size to hydrogen — with valence electrons held tight in compact orbitals. Those three properties together produce a bond with an unusual character [3].

Electron density is pulled hard toward the fluorine, and the bond ends up strongly polarised: a real partial positive charge on carbon, a partial negative charge on fluorine. That charge separation adds an electrostatic attraction on top of the ordinary covalent sharing, so the C–F bond behaves like a covalent bond with an ionic subsidy attached [1]. Meanwhile the fluorine lone pairs, which in any other halogen would be a site of reactivity, are held so tightly they are chemically close to unavailable. Fluorine bound to carbon is a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor and a poor ligand, quiet in a way chlorine, bromine and iodine never are [3].

This is why a perfluoroalkyl chain repels water and oil at the same time, resists heat, oxidation, reduction and light, and is hard to hold on to: with the electrons drawn in tight, a fluorous surface offers only weak dispersion contacts to anything trying to bind it. Keep that last point in mind: it comes back when we get to enzymes.

![Bond dissociation energies across the methyl halides, and how each added fluorine shortens and strengthens the C–F bond](fig1-bond-strength.png)

*Figure 1. Left: bond dissociation energies for the four methyl halides and methane, so the only thing changing is the atom carbon is bonded to: swapping chlorine for fluorine buys roughly 30 kcal/mol of extra strength. Right: the fluoromethane series, where each added fluorine both shortens and strengthens the remaining C–F bonds. Methyl-halide values follow Blanksby & Ellison (2003) [4]; fluoromethane values follow O’Hagan [3] — the two panels are separate compilations, so don't compare CH₃F's value across them.*

## The rule that matters most: fluorine reinforces itself:

Here is the fact that does the most work in PFAS chemistry, and the one most often left out of the introduction: **add more fluorine to a carbon and every C–F bond on that carbon gets stronger.** Walk down the fluoromethane series and the bond dissociation energy climbs steadily (about 110 kcal/mol in CH₃F, 130.5 in CF₄) while the bond itself shortens [3] (Figure 1). Chlorine runs the other way: pile chlorines onto a carbon and the C–Cl bonds get progressively *weaker*, part of why polychlorinated compounds, once written off as undegradable, turned out to be biodegradable after all [2]. Fluorine offers no such favour.

For PFAS the consequence is blunt. A perfluoroalkyl chain is a row of –CF₂– groups with a –CF₃ on the end, and every one of those carbons carries more fluorine than the single fluorinated carbon in fluoroacetate, the one natural substrate enzymes are known to handle well (Figure 2). The chain is not electronically uniform: terminal –CF₃ bonds are generally stronger than internal –CF₂– bonds [5], though which site reacts first depends on mechanism, charge state and environment as much as on bond strength. The only chemically distinctive feature left on a perfluoroalkyl acid is the head group, the carboxylate or sulfonate: the one place the molecule stops being an inert fluorocarbon, and nearly every degradation route anyone has demonstrated goes through it [6].

![Structures of fluoroacetate, difluoroacetate, a fluorotelomer alcohol, and PFOA, showing progressively less for an enzyme to grip](fig2-substrate-comparison.png)

*Figure 2. What an enzyme has to work with. Fluoroacetate is small, carries a charged anchor, and puts its one fluorine on a carbon the neighbouring carboxylate activates. Difluoroacetate adds ≈ 5.8 kcal/mol of bond strength at the same position [7]. In 6:2 fluorotelomer alcohol, two hydrogenated carbons give ordinary microbial oxidation somewhere to begin, which is why telomers degrade and perfluoroalkyl acids do not [2]. PFOA offers none of that: fifteen fluorines, no C–H bond anywhere, nothing polar beyond the head group.*

## Five ways the bond does get broken:

There are more routes than most summaries admit, and each asks something different of the system running it [6] (Table 1).

| Route | How it breaks | What it needs | Where it has been shown |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrolytic Sₙ2 displacement | A carboxylate nucleophile attacks the fluorinated carbon from behind; fluoride leaves as an anion into a purpose-built pocket | No cofactor, no metal, no external energy, just a precisely built active site | Fluoroacetate dehalogenases (α/β-hydrolase fold); some L-2-haloacid dehalogenases; enzymes taking both fluorines off difluoroacetate [1, 8] |
| Reductive, low-potential electrons | Single-electron transfer makes a radical anion that expels fluoride | Reduction potentials as low as −911 mV have been reported for electron-bifurcating systems generally | Perfluorinated unsaturated carboxylic acids reduced by *Acetobacterium* spp.; homologues found in wastewater plants worldwide [9] |
| Oxidative, via a neighbouring handle | An oxygenase attacks a hydrogenated carbon or aromatic ring; defluorination follows from the unstable intermediate | O₂ and a non-fluorinated position to attack; works on polyfluorinated, not perfluorinated, compounds | Fluorotelomer biodegradation; –CF₃ removal from aromatic rings via quinone-methide intermediates [10] |
| Collapse of an unstable intermediate | A *gem*-fluoroalcohol or similar forms, then falls apart on its own, releasing fluoride | Only an enzyme that forms the intermediate; the C–F step itself is uncatalysed | Widely invoked in aerobic biotransformation of polyfluorinated substrates [6] |
| Decarboxylation cascade | Loss of CO₂ generates a perfluoroalkyl carbanion, triggering a run of favourable defluorination steps | A mild base in an aprotic solvent, PFOA itself decarboxylating and mineralising at 80–120 °C, with the decarboxylated intermediate defluorinating further at temperatures as mild as 40 °C; no enzyme yet found, but decarboxylases are ubiquitous | ≥90% defluorination of PFOA and shorter perfluorocarboxylic acids, in vitro [11] |

*Table 1. Five demonstrated routes to C–F cleavage. Only the first has been resolved structurally [1]; the last has so far been shown only in vitro, with no enzyme yet identified [11]. Compiled from [1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 11].*

## Watching an enzyme do it, atom by atom:

The clearest picture of biological C–F cleavage comes from fluoroacetate dehalogenase, from crystal structures of the enzyme RPA1163 from *Rhodopseudomonas palustris*, solved between 1.15 and 1.80 Å. Chan and colleagues trapped it at four points along its reaction (free, substrate-bound, as a covalent intermediate, and product-bound), about as close to a film of enzymatic defluorination as anyone has managed [1].

The enzyme belongs to the α/β-hydrolase family, its active site buried at the interface between the cap and core domains and reachable only along an 11 Å channel. The catalytic machinery is a familiar triad: an aspartate nucleophile (Asp110), a histidine base (His280), a second aspartate (Asp134) holding the histidine in place. But the triad alone doesn't explain defluorination: other dehalogenases share the same fold and nucleophile and mostly can't touch fluorine. The difference is a small, precisely built cavity beside the reacting carbon (Figure 3) [1]. The reaction itself runs in two steps: Asp110 attacks the fluorinated carbon from the side opposite the fluorine (a textbook Sₙ2 displacement), ejecting fluoride and forming a covalent glycolyl–enzyme ester; then His280 activates a water molecule that hydrolyses the ester and regenerates the free enzyme [1].

![The active site of fluoroacetate dehalogenase RPA1163, showing the three residues that converge on the departing fluoride and the 99° attack angle in the crystallised complex](fig3-active-site.png)

*Figure 3. Inside the active site of RPA1163. Left: two arginines clamp the substrate carboxylate, and three residues (His155, Trp156, Tyr219) converge on the fluorine at 3.0–3.3 Å to stabilise it as it departs — a claw reaching for the leaving group. Right: the geometric problem — in the substrate-trapping D110N mutant, the crystallised complex sits at 99° between the C–F bond and the incoming nucleophile, while an Sₙ2 displacement needs 180°, and the reacting carbon has to move 1.4 Å deeper into the site to get there. A bound substrate is not a reaction about to happen. Distances and angles as reported by Chan and colleagues [1].*

The mutational evidence is hard to argue with. Swap Tyr219 for phenylalanine (deleting one hydroxyl group) and turnover on fluoroacetate drops 190-fold. Swap His155 for asparagine, enlarging the pocket without touching its electrostatics, and the enzyme flips its preference: eight times better on chloroacetate than fluoroacetate [1] (Figure 4). Wild type itself prefers fluoroacetate over chloroacetate by roughly fivefold, even though the C–F bond it chooses is about 30 kcal/mol *stronger* than the C–Cl bond it turns down. Bond strength is not what the enzyme is reading. Size is: fluoride has a van der Waals radius of 1.47 Å against 1.75 Å for chloride, and the pocket was built for the small one.

![Turnover of wild-type RPA1163 and five active-site mutants on fluoroacetate versus chloroacetate, showing the preference reversal at His155Asn](fig4-mutant-kinetics.png)

*Figure 4. The enzyme is reading size, not bond strength. Turnover (kₑₐₜ) of wild type and five active-site mutants on fluoroacetate and chloroacetate, log scale. Removing the Tyr219 hydroxyl costs 190-fold in turnover; enlarging the pocket at His155 flips the substrate preference entirely. From the steady-state kinetics reported by Chan and colleagues [1].*

Strip away the detail and the enzyme performs four jobs, none of them “apply force to a strong bond”: it controls local hydration and preorganises the reacting groups, rather than paying to strip a solvation shell off an incoming ion the way a free fluoride nucleophile would need to; it organises nucleophile, carbon and departing fluoride toward the near-attack, collinear geometry an Sₙ2 needs, an arrangement wildly improbable in free solution; it pays for the anion, with three precisely placed hydrogen-bond donors stabilising the fluoride's charge as the water is excluded; and it clears the product: fluoride binds the pocket so weakly that its low affinity favours rapid release to bulk solvent, limiting product inhibition [1]. All four are about the architecture around the bond, not brute force, which is encouraging for anyone hoping to engineer a new defluorinase.

## Why PFAS are so much harder than fluoroacetate:

If enzymes can cleave C–F bonds, and PFAS are built from C–F bonds, why are PFAS still with us? Because nearly everything about a perfluoroalkyl acid is wrong from an enzyme's point of view, and only one item on this list is bond strength.

- **There is no handle.** Fluoroacetate's fluorine sits next to a carboxylate that both activates the carbon and gives the enzyme something charged to grip. PFOA has no such activating group away from the head end, and beyond it there is nothing polar to hold.
- **The bonds are reinforced.** For the reason set out above, every C–F in a perfluoroalkyl chain is stronger than fluoroacetate's. Even so, enzymes from *Dechloromonas*, *Nostoc* and *Polaromonas* strip both fluorines from difluoroacetate at rates comparable to fluoroacetate, so the extra bond strength was never the whole rate limitation people assumed [8]. Nobody yet knows how they manage it.
- **The pocket is the wrong shape.** Fluoroacetate is tiny; a C8 perfluoroalkyl acid is a rigid, bulky rod. Getting one into a buried active site in a productive orientation is a different structural problem, not a harder version of the same one.
- **They behave like surfactants, because they are.** Their amphiphilicity drives strong interfacial partitioning and complicates free substrate concentration; self-association becomes relevant only under concentration- and matrix-dependent conditions well above what's typically found outside a lab [6].
- **They are hard to grip.** A fluorous chain is barely polarisable and offers only weak dispersion contacts [3]. Binding a perfluoroalkyl tail well is genuinely difficult, and binding comes before everything else.
- **The product is a problem too.** Mineralising one PFOA molecule releases fifteen fluoride ions, and the last fragment standing is usually trifluoroacetate, itself more stubborn than what came before it, so the pathway dead-ends instead of closing cleanly [2].

Count how few of those are about bond dissociation energy.

## The other framing: evolution, not chemistry:

The sharpest version of this argument was made directly by Lawrence Wackett in 2024 [2]: PFAS persistence is a biological optimisation problem rather than a chemical one, and the framing matters enormously. Believe the bond is the obstacle and you go hunting for new C–F cleaving enzymes; believe biology is the obstacle and you go to work evolving whole systems around the enzymes we already have [2]. Four observations carry the argument:

- **PFAS are foreign in a way earlier pollutants were not.** Polychlorinated biphenyls were once thought undegradable, until thousands of structurally similar chlorinated natural products turned up, and biology had a head start we didn't know about. Fluorine gives no such head start: polyfluorinated natural products are unknown, and only one native enzyme family, the SAM-dependent fluorinases, is known to catalyse biological C–F bond formation, though multiple homologues have since been characterised [12]. More than seven million structures in PubChem match a broad structural definition of PFAS; 3.6 billion years of evolution ran without a single one of them [2].
- **Degradation needs several inventions at once.** Membrane transport, several sequential C–F cleavages, then something useful made of the remains — and the intermediate steps pay nothing [2].
- **The reward is poor.** PFOA's carbons sit at roughly the oxidation state of carbon monoxide: no reducing power, no nitrogen, no phosphorus to harvest. Compare atrazine, which carries five nitrogens into nitrogen-limited soils and was being degraded by bacteria on six continents within decades of release, driven by real selective pressure. For PFAS that pressure is close to zero [2] (Figure 5).
- **The one product it does make is a poison.** Fluoride can inhibit essential magnesium- and calcium-dependent enzymes at concentrations as low as 0.1 mM, and a survey of three dozen diverse bacteria found no fluorine at all in their elemental composition. Engineered *Pseudomonas putida* expressing a fluoroacetate dehalogenase shows severe fluoride stress under exactly this load; in the *Acetobacterium* work, a strain that naturally carries a deletion in part of its *crcB* fluoride exporter gene simply stopped defluorinating [2, 9]. PFOA would release fifteen fluorides per molecule, not one.

![A four-question comparison of what atrazine had going for it that PFOA lacks, explaining why microbial degradation evolved for one and not the other](fig5-atrazine-vs-pfoa.png)

*Figure 5. Why evolution never built the pathway. Atrazine, the textbook case of biodegradation evolving within decades, satisfies every condition a microbe needs to make a living from a pollutant. PFOA fails almost all of them, and the last is worse than a failure: the reaction poisons the cell that runs it. Following the argument and evidence set out by Wackett [2].*

*An organism that evolved to degrade PFOA would be an organism that evolved to poison itself, slowly, for no reward.*

## So which framing is right?

Both are correct, at different scales, and mixing the scales is what causes the confusion. It is perfectly coherent to say the C–F bond is the strongest single bond in organic chemistry *and* that its strength is not why PFAS persist. The practical split: designing or discovering an enzyme, the chemistry framing tells you what to optimise (stabilising the leaving group, excluding water, attack geometry, binding a fluorous chain at all); making something work in a reactor or a contaminated aquifer, the evolution framing tells you what will actually stop you (uptake, fluoride export, energy supply, whether your organism survives its own success).

## What this means for modelling these systems:

I build computational pipelines for this problem, so here is what the chemistry above implies for modelling, and where the standard workflow quietly misleads people. None of this reports results from ongoing work in the group; these are consequences of published structures and mechanisms.

- **A predicted structure is a pose, not a mechanism.** A docking or co-folding confidence score speaks to structural plausibility, not reactivity — the two aren't reliably related. RPA1163 shows why: a real, high-resolution complex sitting at 99° when the reaction needs 180° [1].
- **Affinity is not turnover.** RPA1163 has a Kₘ of 3.3 mM and turns over about seven times a minute, weak and slow, and it is still the best-characterised defluorinase we have. Ranking candidates by predicted affinity ranks them on the wrong quantity.
- **Measure geometry and occupancy, not a single frame.** What matters is the nucleophile-to-carbon distance, the departure angle, hydrogen-bond donor positioning, and what fraction of a trajectory sits in that arrangement, not whether it ever visits it. Define and report the occupancy criteria; different thresholds give incomparable numbers.
- **Solvent, ions and negative controls matter.** A stray counter-ion or ordered water can make a good-looking pose unreactive. Run known non-defluorinases through the same pipeline: a metric that can't tell them apart from real candidates isn't measuring defluorination.
- **QM/MM gives a barrier in a region you chose, not a verified transition state**, unless the saddle point is actually located and confirmed. Still worth doing, just say so once, clearly.
- **None of it is an assay.** Fluoride release measured by ion-selective electrode or ¹⁹F NMR, mass balance closed, is evidence of defluorination. Everything upstream is a hypothesis with a rank order attached.

## How to read a claim that something degrades PFAS:

The field produces a steady stream of defluorination claims of wildly varying strength. Here is the checklist I run:

- Was fluoride release measured directly (ion-selective electrode, ¹⁹F NMR, ion chromatography), or only inferred from the parent compound disappearing?
- Does the fluorine mass balance close? Parent-compound loss without fluoride release is not evidence of defluorination on its own — sorption, transformation into other organofluorines, and analytical losses all need to be excluded first.
- Were abiotic and heat-killed controls run, and did they show nothing?
- Is the substrate a perfluoroalkyl acid, or a polyfluorinated precursor that still has C–H bonds to work with?
- What fraction of the fluorine came off, and over what period? A few percent in days is a mechanistic clue, not a treatment technology.
- Where did the fluoride go? Was a working fluoride exporter present in whole cells? [9]
- Is trifluoroacetate among the products, and was it counted? It's often the recalcitrant endpoint [2].
- Purified enzyme, defined strain, or undefined consortium? Each supports a different claim.
- Are the concentrations environmentally meaningful: millimolar in a buffer, or nanograms per litre in groundwater?
- Has an independent group reproduced it? In this field, that question has repeatedly turned out to be the decisive one.

None of this is a case for cynicism. A recent preprint reports a haloacid dehalogenase from *Achromobacter mucicolens*, pulled from PFAS-contaminated lake sediment, releasing fluoride from PFOA in a cell-free system (0.55 ppm, a 17% yield, over 24 hours) (Sadik and colleagues, [Research Square preprint](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10043589/v1), not yet peer reviewed). Whether that survives peer review and independent replication is exactly the right question to ask, and asking it carefully is not the same as dismissing the work.

## What would change my mind:

- A native enzyme with real catalytic efficiency against a perfluoroalkyl acid: a kₑₐₜ/Kₘ within a few orders of magnitude of what the same fold achieves on fluoroacetate.
- A structural explanation for the difluoroacetate defluorinases: three homologues handle a stronger, reinforced bond at comparable rates, and nobody knows why yet [8].
- An enzymatic counterpart to the decarboxylation cascade, since decarboxylases are everywhere and the chemistry is already demonstrated in a flask [11].
- A demonstration that fluoride stress can be engineered away: an organism releasing many fluorides per molecule and growing anyway. This is the obstacle I currently regard as the most serious of the four [2].

What would *not* persuade me: more enzymes reported with trace activity on PFAS at yields indistinguishable from sorption plus a good detection limit. We have a number of those already.

## Where this leaves us:

The C–F bond has earned its reputation. It is the strongest single bond carbon forms, it gets stronger the more of it you put on one atom, and it made possible a whole industry of materials that do not break down. Everything said about its strength in the introductions to PFAS papers is true. It is just not the answer to the question those introductions are asking.

Enzymes have been watched cleaving C–F bonds hydrolytically with no energy input at all [1], reductively using the lowest-potential electron carriers in biology [9], and oxidatively by way of neighbouring positions [2]. In a flask, a decarboxylation cascade mineralised PFOA at 80–120 °C, with the decarboxylated intermediate defluorinating further at temperatures as mild as bath water [11]. The barrier for the step itself is unremarkable. What is missing is everything around it: a substrate biology has ever met, a reason to bother metabolising it, several enzymes needed at once, and some way of surviving the fluoride.

That reframing is not a counsel of despair. It is the opposite. If persistence were a bond-strength problem we would be arguing with thermodynamics, and thermodynamics does not negotiate. Because it is an evolution and systems problem, it responds to engineering: directed evolution around the enzymes we already have, fluoride export installed alongside catalytic capacity, co-substrates that pay for the work, and computational design aimed at geometry and leaving-group stabilisation rather than bond energies [2, 6].

**The C–F bond is not the culprit. It is the alibi.**

We have spent two decades explaining PFAS persistence with a number, 130 kcal/mol, that appears in none of the mechanisms by which the bond actually breaks. The real obstacles are less quotable and a good deal more tractable: getting the molecule into the site, holding it in a geometry that has no reason to happen by itself, catching the fluoride on its way out, and keeping the cell alive afterwards. Those are engineering problems. They are hard. They are not forever.

## A tool for this: DeFluorX:

We are soon launching [DeFluorX](https://github.com/KU-MGB/DeFluorX), a single-script pipeline built directly out of the modelling lessons above. Point it at a candidate dehalogenase and it runs the whole screening workflow in one go: AI-driven variant prioritisation, active-site geometry and occupancy checks, WaterMap solvation analysis, molecular dynamics, and QM/MM barrier estimation, combining AI-driven modelling with physics-aware validation instead of ranking candidates on docking score alone. More on it once it is public.
